facts.text: Director Ulli Lommel made this for about $300,000. It reportedly grossed around $25 million, making it one of 1980's biggest indie horror hits.
Distributor The Jerry Gross Organization had three horror hits in 1980: this film, Lucio Fulci's Zombie and Meir Zarchi's I Spit on Your Grave.
Star Suzanna Love (Lacey) was a Dupont heiress who often wrote checks on set to keep her husband Ulli Lommel's movies shooting.
Star Suzanna Love (Lacey) appeared in the film version of Hair (1979) under the name Suki Love, a year before she headlined this slasher for her husband, director Ulli Lommel.
Suzanna Love's brother, Nicholas Love, plays her brother Willy here. Suzanna also co-wrote the script with her husband, director Ulli Lommel.
The blood-soaked face on the British Vipco VHS cover belongs to actor Llewellyn Thomas, who plays Father Reilly in the film.
Before directing this, Ulli Lommel acted for German auteur Rainer Werner Fassbinder and hung around Andy Warhol's Factory. Then he moved to the US and made a slasher.
Suzanna Love, who co-wrote and stars as Lacey, reportedly lined up the Maryland farmhouse where much of the film was shot. It belonged to her aunt.
Producer Albert Zugsmith suggested director Ulli Lommel cast horror legend John Carradine for extra commercial appeal. Carradine's scenes as Dr. Warren were shot in a single day.
In the UK the title was changed to 'The Bogey Man', reportedly because British audiences might not get the American 'Boogey Man' spelling.
John Carradine played Count Dracula in four films, including House of Frankenstein (1944) and House of Dracula (1945). He has 351 film and TV credits.
Richard Scheib of Moria called the film 'oddly lethargic as a slasher', noting it takes nearly half its running time to reach the first victim. He gave it two stars.
The Washington Post's Garry Arnold said the film achieves 'a certain vicious distinction by putting the occasional spectacular kink in an otherwise motley fabric.'
Director Ulli Lommel reportedly played some of the kills for slapstick on purpose, according to Mondo Digital's review of the 2023 4K release.
Director Ulli Lommel said he wanted outrageous killings in an average-looking environment with ordinary actors: first something the audience can identify with, then inject the horror.
Before this film, director Ulli Lommel worked with Andy Warhol, who starred in two of Lommel's films: Cocaine Cowboys (1979) and Blank Generation (1980).
The Montreal Gazette's Bruce Bailey wrote: 'This film is so sick, it ought to be hospitalized-permanently.'
Richard Scheib of Moria called this 'one of the more professional looking efforts' from director Ulli Lommel and 'probably the most well known' of his films.
Filming was in and around Waldorf, Maryland, with extra photography in Los Angeles. The childhood home exterior in La Plata, MD, was badly damaged by a tornado in 2004.
The glowing red eyes on the house exterior nod to The Amityville Horror (1979). The opening nods to John Carpenter's Halloween (1978).
Lommel lit much of the film in heavy reds and blues, echoing John Carpenter and Dario Argento. Mondo Digital also finds traces of The Exorcist and Carrie.
The synthesizer score is by Tim Krog. It was originally credited to a collective called 'Synthe-Sound-Trax.'
Britain's Vipco put this on VHS in November 1981 with a lurid blood-soaked cover. The cover arguably sold more tapes than the film's content justified.
In the UK it got an uncut X certificate in cinemas, yet was later put on the Video Nasties list and pulled from shelves. It was never successfully prosecuted.
Vipco's 1992 UK tape lost 44 seconds, including a bloody topless woman in a bathtub and a dream where Lacey is dragged and tied to a bed. An uncut version arrived in 2000.
In UK cinemas it played as 'The Bogey Man,' a double bill with the 1978 Canadian thriller Blackout, released by Miracle Films in 1981.
Its distributor, The Jerry Gross Organization, was going bankrupt at release, so little of the film's money reached the filmmakers and cast.
A poster for this film appears in the background of Brian De Palma's Blow Out (1981). It was also spoofed in the slasher comedy Student Bodies (1981).
Matt Wavish of Horror Cult Films gave it 8/10. He praised the mirror spirit for causing accidents and suicides instead of standard slasher stabbings.
Leonard Maltin gave it 3 of 4 stars, calling it a combination of The Exorcist and Halloween with effects that are 'quite colorful, if somewhat hokey.'
Los Angeles Times critic Linda Gross called it a 'scary, well-made horror film' and 'a powerful Grand Guignol evocation' of a brother and sister bound by destiny.
The sequel Boogeyman II was shot in 1981 but unreleased until 1983. A third film, Return of the Boogeyman, followed in 1994 and leans heavily on flashbacks.
When Sony released its own Boogeyman in 2005, Ulli Lommel threatened legal action. Sony then reissued his film as 'The Original 1980 Version!'
Actress Jane Pratt, in her first role, is not the Jane Pratt who founded Sassy magazine, though some sources mix them up.
Vinegar Syndrome released a 4K UHD edition in 2023, scanned from the original 35mm camera negative.
